info: "Ag" comes from Latin argentum (silver) — the same root as "argent" in heraldry and the country Argentina, named for silver deposits.
"Au" comes from Latin aurum (gold). "-ous" marks the lower of gold's two common charges (aurous Au⁺ vs. auric Au³⁺) — the old Latin naming system for metals with variable charge.
"Fe" comes from Latin ferrum (iron). "-ous" = lower charge (ferrous Fe²⁺), "-ic" = higher charge (ferric Fe³⁺) — the same Latin pattern as aurous/auric.
Ammonia (NH₃) plus one H⁺. The "-ium" ending marks a cation formed by protonating a neutral molecule — the same pattern as hydronium (H₃O⁺).
From Latin acetum (vinegar) — acetate is the conjugate base of acetic acid, the acid that makes vinegar sour.
The "-ate" suffix marks the standard, most-oxygen-rich oxyanion of an element — here, carbon's main oxygen-containing ion.
Carbonate (CO₃²⁻) plus one H⁺. Often called "bicarbonate" — from an older naming system where "bi-" meant an acid salt, not literally "two hydrogens."
From Greek kyanos (dark blue) — first isolated from Prussian blue pigment, whose color comes from an iron-cyanide compound.
Cyanide (CN⁻) with an oxygen inserted — the "-ate" ending signals the added oxygen, following the usual oxyanion pattern.
"Thio-" (Greek theion, sulfur) means an oxygen has been swapped for sulfur: thiocyanate is cyanate (OCN⁻) with S replacing O.
The "-ate" (more-oxygen) form of nitrogen's oxyanion — the more stable partner to nitrite.
"-ite" means one fewer oxygen than the "-ate" form: nitrite (NO₂⁻) has one less O than nitrate (NO₃⁻).
The "-ate" oxyanion of phosphorus — structurally like nitrate/sulfate, but phosphorus's lower typical oxidation state gives it a 3- charge.
Phosphate (PO₄³⁻) plus one H⁺, which lowers the charge from 3- to 2-.
Phosphate (PO₄³⁻) plus two H⁺ ("di-" = two), lowering the charge from 3- to 1-.
The "-ate" oxyanion of sulfur — same naming pattern as nitrate, phosphate, and carbonate.
Sulfate (SO₄²⁻) plus one H⁺; commonly called "bisulfate."
One fewer oxygen than sulfate — "-ite" again marks the lower-oxygen partner of an "-ate" ion.
Sulfite (SO₃²⁻) plus one H⁺; commonly called "bisulfite."
"Thio-" (sulfur) + sulfate: literally sulfate (SO₄²⁻) with one oxygen swapped for a sulfur atom.
From Greek oxys (sharp/sour), via the plant genus Oxalis (wood sorrel), whose sour taste comes from oxalic acid.
Literally "hydrogen" + "oxide" — one O bonded to one H, named directly for its own composition.
"Per-" here means "extra oxygen": peroxide has an O–O bond not present in a normal oxide, as in hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂).
From Greek chroma (color) — chromium compounds are famous for vivid colors; chromate itself is bright yellow.
"Di-" = two chromate ions fused together (losing a water molecule) — dichromate is the orange form chromate converts to in acid.
"Per-" marks manganese's highest common oxidation state (+7). Permanganate's deep purple color makes it a classic titration indicator.
"Hypo-" (Greek "under") marks the fewest-oxygen member of the per-/-ate/-ite/hypo- family, following the same pattern as the other halogens.
The active ingredient in household bleach. "Hypo-" = fewest oxygens in the chlorine oxyanion ladder: hypochlorite < chlorite < chlorate < perchlorate.
One more oxygen than hypochlorite, one fewer than chlorate — the "-ite" rung of the ladder.
The "-ate" (standard) oxyanion of chlorine — used as an oxidizer in some matches and fireworks.
"Per-" = the most oxygen-rich member of the family. Perchlorate is notably stable despite chlorine's very high oxidation state (+7).
Same "hypo-" (fewest-oxygen) pattern as hypochlorite, one row down the halogen family — bromine instead of chlorine.
The "-ate" oxyanion of bromine — mirrors chlorate, one row down the periodic table.
"Per-" = most oxygen. Unlike perchlorate, perbromate is notoriously hard to synthesize and was a long-standing challenge in inorganic chemistry.
The "hypo-" (fewest-oxygen) member of the iodine oxyanion family.
The "-ate" oxyanion of iodine. Iodate salts are commonly added to table salt as a source of dietary iodine.
"Per-" + "iodate" contracted into one word — the most oxygen-rich iodine oxyanion. Pronounced "per-EYE-oh-date," not "period-ate."

Flagged when this deck was built: this name breaks the per-/-ate/-ite/hypo- pattern the rest of the deck follows, and "fluorite" is actually the mineral CaF₂, not a fluorine oxyanion. Likely a transcription error in the source — worth double-checking against your textbook.
